roots end up inside your drains</h2></div><div class="ansbox"><b class="ab-t">The short answer</b><p>Tree roots get into drains through cracks and joints in the pipe, drawn by the water and nutrients inside. Once in, they grow into a dense mat that catches waste and blocks the line. They are removed by cutting with an electric eel or jetting, and stopped long term by relining the pipe so there are no joints left to enter.</p></div><div class="prose"><p>Roots do not break into sound pipe by force. They find the small openings that already exist. Older Sydney sewers are mostly vitrified clay laid in short lengths, and every joint is a seam. Ground movement, settling and age open those seams slightly, and the warm, moist air leaking from the pipe tells nearby roots exactly where to go.</p><p>A fine root hair enters the joint and finds a constant supply of water. It thickens, branches and spreads along the inside of the pipe, forming a mat that catches paper, wipes and grease. The drain slows, then blocks. Clear it and the roots grow back from the same point, because the joint is still open and the tree is still there.</p><img src="/uploads/tree-root-removal-sydney.jpg" width="1200" height="800" alt="Tree roots removed from a blocked sewer pipe in Sydney" loading="lazy" decoding="async" style="border-radius:14px;margin:6px 0 18px"><p>That is why root problems have two parts: getting the roots out so the drain works today, and deciding what to do about the opening so you are not back here in six months. Our article <a href="/how-do-tree-roots-get-into-sewer-pipes/">how do tree roots get into sewer pipes</a> goes into the detail.</p></div></div></section><section class="section s-light" id="remove"><div class="wrap"><div class="head"><span class="eyebrow">Removal options</span><h2>Options for dealing with tree roots in pipes</h2><p class="lead">Cutting gets the drain working. Sealing stops the roots coming back. Removing the tree is a decision for you and, often, your council.</p></div><div class="tw"><table class="symtable"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Option</th><th scope="col">What it does</th><th scope="col">How long it lasts</th><th scope="col">Best for</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td data-label="Option">Root cutting with an <a href="/services/electric-eel-drain-cleaning/">electric eel</a></td><td data-label="What it does">Cuts the root mass out of the pipe</td><td data-label="How long it lasts">Until the roots regrow, often months</td><td data-label="Best for">Getting a blocked line running now</td></tr><tr><td data-label="Option"><a href="/services/high-pressure-water-jetter/">Hydro jetting</a> with a root nozzle</td><td data-label="What it does">Cuts fine roots and flushes the line</td><td data-label="How long it lasts">Until the roots regrow</td><td data-label="Best for">Lighter roots, flushing after cutting</td></tr><tr><td data-label="Option">Scheduled root cutting</td><td data-label="What it does">Keeps roots trimmed before they block</td><td data-label="How long it lasts">Ongoing, on an interval</td><td data-label="Best for">Where relining is not wanted yet</td></tr><tr><td data-label="Option"><a href="/services/pipe-relining/">Pipe relining</a></td><td data-label="What it does">Seals joints and cracks from inside</td><td data-label="How long it lasts">Long term, no joints to enter</td><td data-label="Best for">Stopping repeat root blockages</td></tr><tr><td data-label="Option"><a href="/services/pipe-replacement/">Pipe replacement</a></td><td data-label="What it does">New pipe with sealed joints</td><td data-label="How long it lasts">Long term</td><td data-label="Best for">Pipes crushed or displaced by roots</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="tnote">Guide only. Any tree near the line can cause trouble if the pipe has an opening.</p></div></div><div class="cause"><span class="cz"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-water"></use></svg></span><div><h3>Dry spells</h3><p>When the soil dries out, roots search harder for water, and the sewer is a reliable source. Root blockages often show up after a dry period.</p></div></div><div class="cause"><span class="cz"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-trowel"></use></svg></span><div><h3>Old clay pipe</h3><p>Clay pipe with mortar or rubber ring joints, common in homes built before modern PVC was standard, offers far more entry points than solvent-welded PVC.</p></div></div><div class="cause"><span class="cz"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-warning"></use></svg></span><div><h3>Neighbour's or street trees</h3><p>Roots do not respect boundaries. Gurgling and slow drainage across several fixtures are common too. A camera inspection confirms roots and shows exactly where they entered.</p></div></details><details class="faq"><summary><span class="fq-mark"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-chev-down"></use></svg></span>Will root killer stop tree roots in my sewer?</summary><div class="fq-body"><p>Root control chemicals can slow regrowth in some cases, but they do not remove an existing root mass and they do not seal the opening the roots came through. Some products can harm the tree or the environment. Cutting followed by relining is the reliable long term fix.</p></div></details><details class="faq"><summary><span class="fq-mark"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-chev-down"></use></svg></span>How often do tree roots grow back after cutting?</summary><div class="fq-body"><p>It varies with the tree, the season and how big the opening is, but regrowth within six to eighteen months is common. Lines with large trees nearby and several open joints tend to need cutting more often. A camera after cutting shows how many entry points there are.</p></div></details><details class="faq"><summary><span class="fq-mark"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-chev-down"></use></svg></span>Should I remove the tree to fix the drain?</summary><div class="fq-body"><p>Removing the tree is not usually necessary to fix the drain. Sealing the pipe with relining stops roots entering even with the tree in place. Tree removal in Sydney often needs council approval, and roots can come from a neighbour's or street tree anyway. acceptedAnswer.text: No. This is drain work, not tree work. We clear the roots out of the pipe and repair the pipe so they cannot get back in. The tree stays where it is. That is usually what people want anyway. Removing a mature tree is expensive, often needs council approval, and does not repair the pipe the roots already damaged.

Into a pipe that has been cleared but not sealed, yes, and usually within a season or two. The roots were drawn to moisture escaping through a crack or an open joint, and cutting them out does not close it. Into a relined section, no, because there is no longer a joint or crack for them to enter through. That is the difference between clearing a blockage and fixing the cause.

mainEntity.name: Can I just have the roots cut out every year?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can, and for some properties it is a reasonable interim position, particularly where a repair is planned but not yet affordable. Scheduled cleaning does exactly this. It is worth understanding what you are buying, though. Each cycle the crack widens a little and the root system behind it grows, so the interval tends to shorten over time rather than stay fixed.

mainEntity.name: Which trees cause the most trouble?

acceptedAnswer.text: The usual pattern is fast-growing species with vigorous surface roots planted close to a drain line, and large established trees whose root spread simply reaches further than people expect. The distance matters less than whether there is moisture escaping from the line. A sound pipe near a large tree is generally left alone. A leaking joint thirty metres away will still be found.

mainEntity.name: How do I know it is roots and not something else?

acceptedAnswer.text: On camera it is unmistakable: roots look like roots. From the fixture it is not, which is why a repeating blockage is worth a camera inspection rather than a third clear. The strongest clue before anyone looks is timing. Grease and build-up get gradually worse. Roots produce a blockage that clears well, behaves for a while, then returns.
